newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British manufacturing expands in May.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British manufacturing expands in May.

text.p: British manufacturing expanded for the 12th month in a row in May, while consumer borrowing grew more slowly than expected in April, according to figures published on Monday.

Economists said the figures provided further evidence of robust economc growth and increased the likelihood that the Bank of England, newly empowered by the Labour government to set monetary policy, might raise interest rates on Friday.
The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply said its purchasing managers' index (PMI) rose to a seasonally adjusted 54.6, its highest level since April 1995, from 53.6 in April.
"Manufacturers again increased output to meet substantial growth in orders," the institute said.

"Buoyant domestic demand from consumers continued to boost order books. Despite a further fall in the rate of growth of export orders, attributed to the sustained strength of the pound, UK manufacturers experienced the fastest growth of total orders since last November."

The survey, sponsored by Reuters, is conducted among purchasing managers in major British companies and is seen as a reliable pointer to official data for industrial production which are published several weeks later.
The strong pound continued to adversely affect manufacturing exports in May but it again reduced the prices of imported materials.
The prices index signalled a further sharp fall in input prices, with a quarter of all manufacturers reporting a fall in prices from a month ago, while only 7.5 percent reported a rise.
There was modest growth in employment.
Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel, said the figures showed Britain's sluggish manufacturers were being helped by the strength of domestic demand, which was offsetting export weakness.
"The case for higher rates is pretty compelling and I think we will see a quarter-point tightening this week," he said.
The Bank of England's interim monetary policy committee meets on Thursday and Friday for its inaugural review of official interest rates, which are now at 6.25 percent.

The central bank said consumer credit grew by a seasonally adjusted 691 million pounds ($1.1 billion) in April after a 793 million pound increase in March but was still up 16.5 percent from a year earlier.
Jeremy Hawkins, economist at Bank of America, said the borrowing figures were much lower than expected.

"This is surprising given the very high level of consumer confidence and may just reflect caution ahead of the election and upcoming budget," he said. "We would expect this to recover over coming months."
M0 money supply grew 6.1 percent in May, compared with 6.0 percent in April, but this represented a slowing compared with recent months.
